title: Chronic heart failure
blurb: Support an adult with chronic heart failure under NICE NG106 (2025): NT-proBNP referral, the four HFrEF medicines, blood test monitoring, advice and rehabilitation.
question: Mr Evans, 70, has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. His MRA dose was increased 10 days ago and today his potassium is 5.8 mmol/L. He also asks whether he must limit his drinks to 1.5 litres a day. What should the nurse do and say?

teach.body: Formally: heart failure is a clinical syndrome of symptoms (breathlessness, fatigue, ankle swelling) and signs caused by a structural or functional heart abnormality; NICE classifies it by left ventricular ejection fraction into reduced (HFrEF), mildly reduced (HFmrEF) and preserved (HFpEF). In plain English: the heart cannot pump or fill well enough, so fluid backs up and the body is short of blood flow. Heart failure is, by definition, symptomatic.

teach.h: Suspected heart failure: NT-proBNP decides the speed
teach.caption: NG106 1.2.3–1.2.7. Obesity, African or African–Caribbean background, diuretics, ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blockers and MRAs can lower NT-proBNP.
Offer all four. ACEi intolerance (not angioedema): ARNI instead. HFmrEF: consider all four. HFpEF: consider an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor.

teach.h: Bloods for ACEi, ARNI, ARB or MRA (NG106 1.7.3–1.7.5)

items.label: If renal function may be compromised

teach.caption: If creatinine rises by more than 50% or potassium rises above 5.5 mmol/L, follow local guidelines. Measure BP before and after each dose increase.

teach.note: Assess heart rate and clinical status after each dose increase. Avoid verapamil, diltiazem and short-acting dihydropyridines in HFrEF.

teach.body: NICE does not routinely advise restricting salt or fluid in heart failure. Ask about intake and advise if needed: a fluid restriction for dilutional hyponatraemia, or reducing very high salt or fluid intake. Advise against potassium-containing salt substitutes. Diuretics relieve congestion and fluid retention and are titrated up and down to the lowest dose needed.

head: Element
NG106
rows: Function, fluid status, pulse, cognition, nutrition, medicines, renal function
Not for advanced heart failure itself

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mr Evans in the heart failure clinic
teach.body: Ten days after his MRA dose increase, Mr Evans's potassium is 5.8 mmol/L: above the 5.5 mmol/L level at which NG106 says follow local guidelines. Heart failure nurse Sam does not simply carry on; she checks his ECG and observations and escalates to the prescriber the same day. She asks about salt substitutes (he uses one containing potassium) and advises stopping it. On fluids, she explains NICE does not routinely restrict them, and agrees advice based on his actual intake.

teach.text: Old practice vs NG106 2025: medicines are NOT started one at a time, each fully optimised before the next. NICE now offers all four HFrEF medicines and says it is not necessary to optimise one dose before introducing another. And routine salt and fluid restriction is not advised.

items: NT-proBNP above 2,000: echo and specialist within 2 weeks; 400–2,000: within 6 weeks.
HFrEF: ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker + MRA + SGLT2 inhibitor together (ARNI if ACEi intolerant).
U&E before starting, 1–2 weeks after starting and each increase, then 3–6 monthly.
Act on potassium above 5.5 mmol/L or creatinine up more than 50%.
No routine salt or fluid restriction; no potassium salt substitutes; flu jab yearly; cardiac rehab.

summary: You can now apply NG106 2025 to chronic heart failure: NT-proBNP referral timeframes, the four HFrEF medicines, blood and BP monitoring with action thresholds, and beta-blocker safety checks. You can also give accurate advice on salt, fluid, vaccination and cardiac rehabilitation.

A.q: A woman with suspected heart failure has an NT-proBNP of 2,600 ng/L. Within what timeframe should she have specialist assessment and echocardiography?
A.why: NG106 1.2.3: NT-proBNP above 2,000 ng/L means urgent referral for specialist assessment and transthoracic echo within 2 weeks.

whyNot.0: 24 hours is not the NG106 timeframe for this level.
whyNot.3: 3 months is too slow for this level.

A.q: Which combination does NG106 (2025) recommend offering to people with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
options: ACEi, ARB, loop diuretic and digoxin
ARB, aspirin, statin and a nitrate
A.why: NG106 1.4.1 (2025): offer an ACE inhibitor, a beta-blocker, an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor to people with HFrEF.

whyNot.0: ACEi and ARB together is not the NG106 combination, and digoxin is for worsening HF despite optimised treatment.
whyNot.1: Verapamil should be avoided in HFrEF.
whyNot.2: This is not the HFrEF treatment combination.

A.q: What advice does NG106 give about salt and fluid for a man with stable heart failure and normal sodium?
options: Restrict fluids to 1.5 litres a day
Swap to a potassium salt substitute
Ask about intake; no set limit
Restrict salt intake to 2 g a day
A.why: NG106 1.9.10: do not routinely advise restricting sodium or fluid; ask about intake and advise if needed (e.g. fluid restriction for dilutional hyponatraemia).

whyNot.0: Routine fluid restriction is not advised; it is for specific cases such as dilutional hyponatraemia.
whyNot.1: Potassium-containing salt substitutes should be avoided (1.9.11).
whyNot.3: NICE does not set a routine salt restriction figure.

B.q: A man has just started ramipril and spironolactone for HFrEF. When should his renal function and electrolytes next be checked?
B.why: NG106 1.7.4: measure renal function and electrolytes 1 to 2 weeks after starting treatment and after each dose increment.

whyNot.1: 3–6 monthly checks apply once the maximum tolerated dose is established.
whyNot.2: Annual checks are far too infrequent after starting these drugs.
whyNot.3: 6 to 8 weeks is later than NG106 advises.

B.q: Before a beta-blocker is prescribed for heart failure, which test does NG106 recommend?
B.why: NG106 1.7.10: assess heart rhythm, rate and conduction abnormalities with a 12-lead ECG before deciding to prescribe a beta-blocker.

whyNot.0: A chest X-ray does not show conduction problems.
whyNot.2: COPD is not a reason to withhold a beta-blocker, and spirometry is not the required test.
whyNot.3: A urine collection is not relevant to beta-blocker safety.

B.q: Which finding means a beta-blocker should not be offered under NG106?
B.why: NG106 1.7.11: do not offer a beta-blocker to people with bradycardia (heart rate below 50/min) or 2nd/3rd-degree heart block without a pacemaker.

whyNot.0: Age is not a reason to withhold a beta-blocker (1.7.9).
whyNot.1: COPD is not a reason to withhold a beta-blocker.
whyNot.3: Diabetes is not a reason to withhold a beta-blocker.

C.q: Mrs Gill, 77, with HFrEF, had her ramipril dose increased 2 weeks ago. Her creatinine has risen from 100 to 165 micromol/L. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
options: Record it and recheck in 3 months
Give an extra dose of furosemide
Advise her to drink 3 litres daily
C.why: A rise from 100 to 165 is more than 50%. NG106 1.7.5: if creatinine rises by more than 50% or potassium rises above 5.5 mmol/L, follow local guidelines, which means prompt escalation to the prescriber.

whyNot.0: A rise of over 50% needs action now, not routine follow-up.
whyNot.2: Extra diuretic could worsen renal function.
whyNot.3: A large fixed fluid intake is not the response and may cause overload.

C.q: Mr Okoro, 69, with HFrEF, is on the maximum tolerated doses of an ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor but remains symptomatic. What does NG106 suggest considering?
options: Adding an ARB to the ACE inhibitor
Switching the ACEi to an ARNI
C.why: NG106 1.4.2: for people on the maximum tolerated dose of each of the 4 medicines who still have symptoms, consider switching the ACE inhibitor to an ARNI (allowing at least 36 hours after the last ACEi dose).

whyNot.0: Combining an ACEi and an ARB is not the NG106 approach.
whyNot.1: Diltiazem should be avoided in HFrEF.
whyNot.2: Stopping a beta-blocker removes a key HFrEF medicine.

C.q: A heart failure nurse is planning discharge for Mrs Hart, 81, after an admission with decompensated HFrEF. Which recommendation is part of NG106 ongoing care?
options: Long-term home oxygen for her breathlessness
C.why: NG106 1.11.1: offer a personalised, exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme, preceded by an assessment and in an accessible format.

whyNot.0: NG106 1.12.1: do not offer long-term home oxygen for advanced heart failure.
whyNot.2: Routine fluid restriction is not advised.
whyNot.3: Stable patients are reviewed at least every 6 months.

reteach.title: Four pillars and two blood numbers
reteach.question: What is the simplest way to remember the 2025 HFrEF treatment and its main safety checks?

blocks.h: Build all four pillars, watch two numbers
blocks.body: Picture a roof held up by four pillars: an ACE inhibitor, a beta-blocker, an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor. NICE now puts all four up together rather than one at a time. Three of the drugs that act on the kidneys and potassium (ACEi, ARNI/ARB, MRA) need bloods 1–2 weeks after starting and after each increase. Watch two numbers: potassium above 5.5 mmol/L and creatinine up by more than 50%.

blocks.text: Potassium salt substitutes plus an MRA plus an ACE inhibitor can push potassium dangerously high: advise people with heart failure to avoid them.

explain.body: History, examination and NT-proBNP. Above 2,000 ng/L: echo and specialist within 2 weeks. 400–2,000: within 6 weeks. Below 400 in an untreated person: HF less likely.

test.q: A man with suspected heart failure has an NT-proBNP of 900 ng/L. Within what timeframe should echo and specialist assessment happen?
test.why: NG106 1.2.4: NT-proBNP between 400 and 2,000 ng/L: specialist assessment and echo within 6 weeks.

whyNot.0: 48 hours is not an NG106 timeframe.

explain.body: HFrEF: offer ACEi, beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor. ACEi intolerance other than angioedema: ARNI instead. Angioedema with ACEi: beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i and consider an ARB.

items.label: gap from last ACEi to first ARNI

test.q: A woman with HFrEF developed angioedema on an ACE inhibitor. Which approach fits NG106?
options: Start an ARNI in place of the ACEi
Restart the ACEi at a lower dose
test.why: NG106 1.4.4: after angioedema with an ACEi, offer a beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor and consider an ARB.

whyNot.0: An ARNI is the alternative for ACEi intolerance other than angioedema.
whyNot.1: Restarting the drug that caused angioedema is unsafe.
whyNot.3: This omits the core HFrEF medicines.

explain.body: U&E before starting ACEi/ARNI/ARB/MRA, 1–2 weeks after starting and after each increase, then every 3–6 months. BP before and after each increase. Heart rate after each beta-blocker increase.

test.q: Once a patient is on the maximum tolerated dose of an MRA, how often should renal function and electrolytes be checked?
test.why: NG106 1.7.4: every 3 to 6 months once the maximum tolerated dose has been established, and any time renal function may be compromised.

whyNot.0: Weekly checks are for the period after changes, not long term.
whyNot.2: Two-yearly checks are far too infrequent.

explain.body: Ask about salt and fluid; no routine restriction. Avoid potassium salt substitutes. Influenza vaccine yearly, pneumococcal once. Exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation. Review at least every 6 months when stable.

test.q: How often should a person with heart failure be offered pneumococcal vaccination under NG106?
test.why: NG106 1.9.8: offer pneumococcal vaccination (required once); influenza vaccination is annual.

whyNot.1: Five-yearly boosters are not the NG106 advice.
whyNot.3: Ten-yearly boosters are not the NG106 advice.
